Simbi 源於班圖語與剛果語社群，詞源可能出自基剛果語「持有、保存」；十七世紀: Simbi belongs to Bantu and Kongo-speaking communities, and the word may come from the Kikongo for “to hold, to keep”; seventeenth-century dictionaries of early Kongo already record phrases such as “a respected person in the community” and “one who does not die of old age”, which shows its link between the world of the living and that of the ancestors. The Atlantic slave trade forced more than twelve and a half million people to move, and the worship travelled with them to the United States, Brazil, Cuba and Haiti. In the nineteenth century Edmund Ruffin recorded encounters with water spirits in South Carolina; Hoodoo tradition sees them as guardians of streams and of fertility, and Haitian Vodou and Cuban Palo also keep Kongo beliefs in nature spirits.

The left hand stops the strings or changes the sounding length to control pitch, the right hand sets the strings vibrating. A chordophone works by passing the string's vibration into a soundbox that amplifies it. Pluck with a fingertip or a pick, and watch the angle of contact and the force.
辛比琴主要採用天然材質製作。共鳴箱通常由非洲傳統木材如桃花心木或相思木製成，提供: The simbi is made mostly of natural materials. The resonator is usually of traditional African woods such as mahogany or acacia, which give a warm sound. The strings are of natural animal gut or plaited plant fibre and resonate well. The decoration may be inlaid with bone, ivory or shell. Some versions add metal parts to brighten the timbre. The whole design emphasises combinations of natural materials and keeps the character of the original craft.
辛比琴的音色具有獨特的靈動與神秘質感。其音色明亮而富有穿透力，帶有清澈的高頻特徵: The simbi's timbre has an unusual liveliness and mystery. It is bright and penetrating, with a clear high-frequency character, and warm middle layers as well. Its range is broad and it can produce a rich variety of pitch from high and piercing to low and deep. It resonates in its own way: the vibration of the strings through the resonator gives a warm sound with body to it and a slight nasal quality. Beside the clean timbre of the modern guitar the simbi seems older and rawer; beside the harp it has more local character and mystery. Its sound holds the breath of the natural world, with both a metallic sheen and wooden warmth, and it can create a listening experience that is ethereal and close at hand at once.

Simbi (also spelled Cymbee and Sim'bi, plural Bisimbi or Basimbi) is a spirit that guards water and nature in the traditional Bakongo religion of Central Africa, and it is also found in the spiritual traditions of the African diaspora, such as rootwork (Hoodoo) in the southern United States and Palo in Cuba. Historically the simbi were thought to take the form of water-dwelling people or mermaids, pottery, snakes, gourds and fire. Because of the Atlantic slave trade, large numbers of Bantu people were bought, sold or seized from Africa and taken to the Americas.
